utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Have the accused brought in, please. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good morning to the interpreters, good morning to counsel, both Defence and Prosecution, to the accused. We can now resume our work at the point that we left off. Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Our next witness is Mr. Mato Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to raise a point of order, and that is that Mr. Tadic was given to us as a potential witness, his name, six days ago, and the ruling of this Chamber is that the Prosecutor should be apprised seven days in advance before a witness is called. I received a fax from the Defence on the 12th of January at 7.30 or 7.23 in the evening. Now, I am perfectly happy to have this witness proceed, but we have also received the names of other witnesses seven days in advance, and we prepare in accordance with the Rule that requires us to have seven days notice in advance. So, obviously, we are somewhat disadvantaged in the cross-examination of this witness. We are happy to have him proceed today, but we may ask that he remain until tomorrow for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I am not mistaken, today is the 19th. Counsel is saying he got notice on the evening of the 12th. Count backwards, 19, 18, 17, 16, 15, 14, 13, 12. It's seven days. What happened on the 12th of January? We had a Status Conference concerning Judge Riad. We didn't know if we were going to proceed or not this week. We were in Court until 5.00 or 6.00 on the 12th, and I went home to my office from Court that morning and I typed up the disclosure and I faxed it straightaway to the Prosecutor. I was still working at 7.30 or 8.00, whenever it was, on the night of the 12th, and I worked that evening to send that notice after the Court's hearing. So that's our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think that we'd have to try to see things relatively. The Prosecutor says that he didn't have the seven days. I'm not sure how you are calculating. I know you all know how to calculate properly. You know that 12 and 7 is 19. If we start from the evening of the 12th -- the evening of the 19th. All right. Please. Yes, there were some organisational problems having to do with Judge Riad's unavailability. Will you be prepared for the cross-examination today? If you aren't -- will you be ready? If you aren't, we can give you more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can let you know after I hear what this witness has to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Then we can wait. All right. Let's have the witness brought in for the time being. Let me point out to you that the Judges are not seeing their transcript on the monitors. One of the Judges can see the transcript. Of course, it's always in English. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: It's because it's in English. That's what my colleague is pointing out to me. All right. Do you hear me, sir? Please remain standing. Give us your first name, your date and place of birth, your profession and your residence, and then you will take an oath and then you will be seated. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Mato Tadic. I was born on the 15th of August, 1952 in Brcko. I now reside in Sarajevo in Muhamed Hadzijahic Street, number 43. Up until the 15th of December, 1998, I worked in the Government of the Federation as Minister of Justice. At present I am on holiday and I am using the rights accorded me by the law on state administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Please take the oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you known as Your Excellency, the minister or sir or Mr.?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think Mr. Tadic would be best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Tadic. Thank you very much. You have agreed to testify for the Defence, the Defence of the accused, General Blaskic, who was a Colonel at the time, who has been accused of various crimes. You are going to answer the questions first of the Defence attorneys who brought you here, and then the Prosecution will ask you some questions, and then possibly the questions that the Judges may care to ask as well. Mr. Nobilo, proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Tadic, you have also said you were born in 1952 in Brcko. Can you tell us something about your education, where you went to school, when you completed primary school, secondary school and university?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: After completing primary school in Brcko, I went to the Franciscan classical gymnasium in Visoko. Visoko is a town some 30 kilometres southwest of Sarajevo. Having completed gymnasium, I went to the theological faculty of Sarajevo for two years, and after that the faculty of law of the university in Sarajevo where I graduated in the 1st of June, 1977. Having graduated, I returned to Brcko, where I started work in the Municipal Office of the Prosecutor, Public Prosecutor, and after passing my exams, legislative exams, I was the Deputy Public Prosecutor. From 1983, for eight years, I was the Public Prosecutor. From the 1st of January, 1991, I have been Deputy Republic Prosecutor for Bosnia and Herzegovina. That is where I was when the war broke out in 1992. On the 28th of April, 1992, I left Sarajevo and went to Brcko, where I spent only one day and one night. After that I withdrew to the territory that was organising resistance to the Yugoslav People's Army and the Serbian Army in the area of Brcko, after which I went through several places in Posavina to the north of Bosnia-Herzegovina. These places were Odzak, Bosanski Brod. After that, at the end of 1992, in December, in fact, I came to Orasje, that is a town to the north of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which is where I spent the entire year of 1993. My task was to set up the work of the courts and Prosecutors' offices and the legal authorities and to set up the civilian institutions of parent authority. From Orasje, at the end of February or the beginning of March, 1994, I went to Mostar to the Ministry of Justice and of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. On the 30th of March I was in Sarajevo once again to the assembly, constitutional assembly, of the Federation after the Washington Accords. On the 22nd of June, 1994, I was appointed to the government of the Republic and Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the government of Prime Minister Silajdzic. And this was one government with a dual role, the role of republic and the role of federation. After that, I was appointed to two more governments of the federation, on the 1st of February, 1996 and on the 18th of December, 1996, and I performed my duties up until the 15th of December, 1998. I took part in a series of international conferences as a legal expert, conferences linked to Bosnia-Herzegovina. The most important was the Dayton conference. In the preparations for the Dayton conference, I spent some time in New York, and then I was in Dayton for the entire time as a legal expert and at several other conferences in London, Vienna, Rome, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. May we now, after that introduction, move on to the topic for which we have invited you here today to testify as a Defence witness. Can you tell us something about the legislative setup of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the fate of that system, legal system, at the beginning of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: The legal system of Bosnia-Herzegovina had certain rules and regulations governing it which were republican, that is to say, of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, such as the law on courts and the law on public prosecutors' offices and some material rules and regulations. However, at the same time in ex-Yugoslavia, we had all the process laws at the level of Yugoslavia, for example, the Law on Criminal Procedure, and we also had other material rules and regulations such as the Criminal Code, the Penal Code, the special part of it relating to individual military matters, security matters, and others relating to perpetrators in federal organs, perpetrators of crimes in federal organs. After the war broke out in Bosnia-Herzegovina in April, and especially later on in May 1992, there was a complete state of chaos in the legal system and in law, and part of Bosnia-Herzegovina became separated, that is to say, it became an autonomous setup with regard to legal matters, the legal system. That is the portion that was in the Republika Srpska. The second half, the second part, functioned under difficult conditions, and the presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in order to establish the functioning of a legal system, enacted a number of provisions having the force of law so that it took over the Law on Criminal Procedure that was prevalent in Yugoslavia and enacted a second rule and regulation taking over the law from the one that existed in Yugoslavia and rules as to its application in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Some of the laws, as I have already said, the republics did not have. For example, the law on military courts did not exist, and the law governing military prosecution, these exclusively existed at the federal level, that is to say, at the level of Yugoslavia. And for this reason, the presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, by a decree, set up these military courts in Bosnia-Herzegovina and also military prosecutors' offices. This decree was enacted on the 13th of August, 1992, and it was published in the official gazette, number 12/92. According to that decree, for the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, seven military courts were set up. They were in Bihac, Banja Luka, Doboj, Tuzla, Zenica, Sarajevo, and Mostar. Therefore, this decree encompassed the whole territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, regardless of the fact that part of the territory had already severed the hierarchial cooperation that it had with the Supreme Court in Sarajevo, and that is the section that was in the Republika Srpska. At the end of 1992, because it was impossible to communicate and because all communications had been severed, the Supreme Court formed its own departments outside Sarajevo, and they were in Tuzla, Bihac, Mostar, and Zenica. Also at the end of 1992 in the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, a decree was enacted to set up military courts and military prosecutors' offices, and by that decree, four military courts were formed in Mostar, Livno, Travnik, and Bosanski Brod. Therefore, already at the end of 1992, we had three legal legislative systems, and very soon, we would be given a forth in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that would be the one set up under the control of Fikret Abdic in Western Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Before we move on, I should like to have a set of documents handed out which testify to the decisions made by Herceg-Bosna to set up these courts of law.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is D521A for the French version and "B" for the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, would you please take a look at the documents that we have tendered into evidence as D521 and tell us whether those documents are the ones that set up the district courts in Herceg-Bosna and the offices of the prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: For the moment, we are not going to enter into detail, we'll be doing that later on when we speak about procedure, criminal procedure, but could you, at this point, tell us why, in your opinion, although you were not in Mostar at the time and did not take part in drawing up these laws, why were the military courts set up in Herceg-Bosna, as the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina had established seven military courts of law for the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina previously?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: Well, you would have to know the circumstances that prevailed in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time, and then you would be able to understand the necessity for enacting provisions of this kind. When the war broke out, an essential characteristic was that the communication lines were cut off between the main centres in Bosnia-Herzegovina, first of all, between Sarajevo as the capital and the headquarters of the institutions of the republic, and also communications were severed with the other large centres such as Tuzla, Bihac, Mostar, Zenica, let alone Banja Luka and Doboj, which were constantly under the control of the army of Republika Srpska. Secondly, in this territory, apart from the Yugoslav People's Army, there was no professional army. There were no military courts that had previously existed. They were established at the level of Yugoslavia, and, therefore, we had to find a solution for this newly arisen situation. As the armies organised themselves and tried autonomously, independently, even one from the other, and that discipline had to be maintained and disciplinary action taken, then this had to be regulated on the basis of rules and regulations, and the Croatian Defence Council, which was established fairly early on, even before the army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina had been set up, and, second, in the decree of the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina is mentioned in precise terms, all of which indicated the need for a decree to regulate matters of criminal liability and disciplinary action within the Croatian Defence Council, and this was a basic reason for which these rules and regulations were adopted, and it was adapted to the organisation of the Croatian Defence Council itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Before we move further on, can we take a look at these documents and at Article 1, and I'm going to read it: "In time of war on the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, herein HZHB, military district courts shall be established." How do you understand that article of the provision?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: From the norms of this provision, it clearly shows that this is of a temporary nature, provisional, only during the state of war and that it is a necessary provision resulting from the outbreak of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us, please, district military courts in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, at what level was work in these courts done, and did these courts recognise the Supreme Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is to say, the joint court for the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and if so, how did this manifest itself?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: The district military courts of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna were courts of the first instance, and they covered certain areas, certain territories, that is to say, a number of municipalities. What is characteristic for these courts is the fact that the hierarchy with respect to decision making made by the district military courts were under the competence of the civilian courts of law, and that means that if there were any complaints to be made and appeals for crimes committed and sentenced up to five years' imprisonment to a higher court, which was a civilian court of law and which had existed previously, and in more serious cases, appeals were made to the Supreme Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina and its department, regional department or branch office in Mostar; therefore, we retained the hierarchial competence of the civilian courts over the military courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that these were civilian courts which functioned in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which were functioning there before the war and which were common to everybody in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is to say, on the basis of the laws that prevailed at the time?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, these were civilian courts functioning on the basis of regular laws governing the regular law courts and the public prosecutors' offices. And in Article 5(B) of this particular provision, it is clearly stated that appeals, as I say, appeals, against decisions be decided by the Supreme Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina or its detached chamber of the Supreme Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina seated in Mostar, and it also states that this should be resorted to when there is severed communications between the Supreme Court, that is to say, when communication with the Supreme Court in Mostar for Bosnia-Herzegovina was not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, as regards court administration and also ensuring conditions for the operation of courts and also for the court budget and other logistic support, what is the hierarchy involved, and under whose jurisdiction were the military courts in terms of court administration and material functioning of the courts?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: District military courts were under the jurisdiction, under the competence, of the defence department, that is to say, civilian authorities that were then called the defence department, so they were in charge of the court administration and logistics, that is to say, ensuring conditions for their proper operation and also making sure that salaries could be paid.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, could you please explain to the Court about the judges and the prosecutors? What status did they have and who appointed military judges and military prosecutors?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: Article 2 of this decree says that district military courts shall perform their functions independently and shall operate on the basis of the constitution and law. May I recall that at that time we had one constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and as far as appointments are concerned, that was resolved in Article 20 of the same decree.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You mean the decree on military courts?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the decree I'm talking about, so I'm talking about Article 20 where it says, "The judges and jurors of the district military courts shall be elected and relieved of office by the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna as proposed by the head of the Defence Department," and they also submitted reports on their work to the presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, according to your interpretation and your perception of the work of military courts, the commander of an Operative Zone, in this specific case, Colonel Blaskic, who was subordinated to the main staff, did he have anything to do with the establishment of courts, the appointment of judges, the control over the work of courts or military prosecutors' offices, and the like?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: No, no, it is the defence department that had this right. There is a specific provision stipulating that, at the proposal of the defence department, the presidency does this, and there are specific provisions to this effect, so in this respect, he did not have any competencies whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The next point that I wish to hear your views on, I would like you to present them to the Court, and that is criminal procedure. What was criminal procedure like in accordance with the Law on Criminal Procedure, and when was this law of Yugoslavia taken over by Bosnia and Herzegovina in order to become a law of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Herceg-Bosna, and what were the stages involved in this procedure?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: I pointed out earlier on, when I was presenting a brief survey of the justice system, that at the level of Yugoslavia we had a single procedural law as regards criminal procedure. That was the Law on Criminal Procedure, and the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina took it over. This was a decree with legal force and it was published in the Official Gazette No. 2/92, 6/92 and 9/92. Lest there be any misunderstanding, may I just clarify this a bit. Technically, this was taken over on a double track so-to-speak. Once a decree on the takeover of the Law on Criminal Procedure of the former Yugoslavia was passed, and then another decree was passed on the application and implementation of the Law on Criminal Procedure, notably, on its implementation in cases of war or imminent danger of war. Because some things were simply resolved differently in cases of war and imminent danger of war. That is why there were so many Official Gazettes in which this was published. Also, at the same time the Criminal Code was taken over, both the general provisions and the special provisions, along with certain corrections, and this was also published in the Official Gazette of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina 2/92, 8/92 and 10/92. So the Law on Criminal Procedure now became a republican law and, to the best of my recollection, certain chapters are being implemented, notably, Chapter 15 of the Law on Criminal Procedure which speaks of so-called previous procedure. That is to say criminal charges being filed against someone and someone acting according to these criminal charges filed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Please tell the court, according to the Law on Criminal Procedure which applied in Yugoslavia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Herceg-Bosna, who is entitled to file criminal charges against someone and where are these criminal charges filed?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: First of all, there is a general provision saying that every citizen is entitled to bring criminal charges against someone. However, in practice, and I personally studied this particular matter, 90 per cent of all criminal charges in the former Yugoslavia and Bosnia-Herzegovina were filed by the police authorities in charge, and only 10 per cent were filed by all the rest, that is to say individual citizens, enterprises, companies, institutions, et cetera. That is to say criminal charges were mainly brought forth by the police, that is to say their crime investigation services that actually filed these criminal reports, made them up, and saw where there were elements of crime. That is the way in which they filed criminal charges against someone, along with evidence, and they did this to the Prosecutor's office. Then it was the Public Prosecutor who received these criminal reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that we have a termological problem in the English language. My colleague Mr. Hayman says so. He says that "criminal report" is being interpreted as "criminal charges brought against." My colleague, Mr. Hayman, believes that "criminal charges" are the same thing as an "indictment," and we are not speaking about indictments. We are talking about criminal reports filed by citizens to the police. So perhaps "complaint" would be a better term, not "charges brought against," but "complaint lodged." Because every citizen, every institution can write a paper saying "my neighbour stole my car yesterday," and he sends that paper to the police. So that is a criminal complaint. That is not a formal paper involved in the criminal procedures. So perhaps, termologically, we should use a different word for this. We should use "criminal complaint."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Can you ask the witness to explain this. The police could file a complaint in the court against someone. Whether you call that complaint a complaint or an indictment does not matter for present purposes. What I should like to know from you, through the witness, is this: Could a private citizen directly file a complaint in the court against another citizen or is a private citizen limited to this, that he must file a report with the police and leave it to the police to consider whether or not they would file a formal complaint in the court? Is my question clear to you, Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: It is quite clear, and we have a highly qualified person to answer these questions, because the system is substantially different from that prevailing in Anglo-Saxon law, and therefore it is very important to explain who is entitled to lodge such a criminal complaint and who it is addressed to.

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: There is no problem whatsoever. I am going to explain it to you in detail, because I am one of the persons who worked on this for years in this kind of a system, I mean. An individual citizen can and does lodge a complaint, in terms of a specific criminal offence, primarily to the police. Then the police processes the matter involved. An individual citizen can address a court of law directly only in a few very special cases. These are so-called private suits for lesser forms of incrimination, for example, for insults, libel, insult and libel. Also, some other offences which are of a purely private nature belonging to the domain of the family, for instance, and where it is up to the citizen whether he is going to lodge a complaint with the court. This is called a private suit and, in this case, the court of law is addressed directly. In all other cases, I am talking about criminal offences now, the citizen, the private citizen cannot appear before a court. He has two options. One is to report the event concerned to the police and then to have the police process this, to cooperate with the police in terms of finding the perpetrator, if the perpetrator is unknown, and also in terms of collecting evidence. The other option that the citizen can resort to is directly addressing the Public Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. In order to clarify matters, am I right if I say that the Public Prosecutor's office is structurally, organisationally separate from the court, it is a different institution from the actual court?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes. In our country the Public Prosecutor's office is an independent state organ quite separate from the court of law. That is one of the differences between our law and Anglo-Saxon law and even the set-up of laws in some other western countries. In our country the role of the Public Prosecutor is different than that in the Anglo-Saxon system and also in some other western European systems. An individual citizen could come to the Public Prosecutor's office and say that his car had been stolen and then a so-called report is written out on that. Also the citizen concerned is cautioned against perjury and usually the evidence involved is poor. Then the Public Prosecutor resorts to Article 153 of the Law on Criminal Procedure, paragraph 2, and then the Prosecutor asks the police or other authorities to have certain data, evidence, submitted to him to interview certain witnesses. These are so-called information interviews. Also, they do not have the weight of evidence before a court of law. However, the Prosecutor can use this when weighing his options and seeing whether he is going to institute an investigative proceedings or not. I don't know if I've been clear on this point and whether this has been sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, I am content.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, please tell the court who can give instructions either to the civilian or to the military police to take certain action, to conduct pre-criminal proceedings, to interview a person? So who are the persons who can give such instructions to the police according to law?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: First of all, we must take as a point of departure the fact that the police has a hierarchy of its own, and it has its own bosses, so-to-speak. They say what is going to be done. They give guidelines. That is one part of it. The other part is one that can exist, according to the Law on Criminal Procedure, and it is the Public Prosecutor in this particular case, and he is also duty bound in a way to do so. If he asks the police to work out such a report and if he studies this report, and if he assesses that some things remained unclear, and therefore procedure cannot be continued and he cannot address himself to the court, then he resorts to Article 153, paragraph 2 of the Law on Criminal Procedure and asks the police or someone else. He is also entitled to ask other institutions for certain pieces of information, documents. For example, a sketch of the crime scene, photographs, analyses, blood analyses, for example. This can help him make an assessment as to whether he is going to enter the formal part of the procedure, that is to say vis-a-vis the court of law.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, what about the investigation judge? Can the investigation judge also give the police instructions in order to carry out certain pre-investigation actions?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There are explicit powers to that effect in the Law on Criminal Procedure. They were somewhat more liberal during the war, for practical reasons, because the police were more operational in this way. It was easier for them to get to the crime scene, for example, et cetera, and the investigation judge could check that's what the Law on Criminal Procedure says. That is to say that he could entrust the police with carrying out certain things. Some action can only be ordered by the investigation judge, not by the Prosecutor, not by the police, and that is exhumation and a post-mortem. This is exclusively the right of the investigation judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So you mentioned three groups of persons who can give instructions to the military police to take action, that is, the investigation judge, the Public Prosecutor and senior police officers. Now I am asking you the following: The commander of the Operative Zone, Colonel Blaskic, could he order the military police to take fingerprints, for example, to interview persons, to question certain persons or to do anything else by way of pre-criminal proceedings, anything of this nature?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: In order to give an answer to this question of yours, one has to know how the military police was set up. It is a special administration within the Ministry of Defence, and it has a commander of its own, it has its own head. Within, this military police has a few segments, for example, the crime investigation service, the security service, the traffic and communication service, transport and communication service, in that sense. This was under the jurisdiction of the head of the military police, within this hierarchy of the establishment of the military police. So Mr. Blaskic did not have these powers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We are going to go back to the documents later on, but we are going to try and present the procedure, the criminal procedure in Bosnia-Herzegovina. When a case, according to the opinions of the police, that the case is being completed, that the perpetrators have been uncovered, that enough evidence has been amassed, what does the police do then? Where does it send this case onto then?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: The whole case is then sent onto the Public Prosecutor. It is referred to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What decisions can the Public Prosecutor take once he receives the case from the police?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: The Public Prosecutor studies the report that he has received from the police and he can undertake the following steps. First he can reject it. Article 153, paragraph 1 of the ZKP, Law on Criminal Procedure, provides for this, because the Prosecutor feels that the report does not constitute a criminal act, or he feels that the material offered, for example, that the case is out of date and there are formal reasons which can lead him to reject a case. Or that there is no reasonable doubt that a case exists, that is to say that there is not even the minimum of evidence necessary to bring in a case of this kind and to try it further. Second, the Public Prosecutor is faced with a dilemma, because, for example, what the police have sent him is not a complete report. He doesn't feel it to be complete. Then relating to Article 153, paragraph 2, as far as I remember, of the Law on Criminal Procedure, he seeks prior information, preliminary information. That is the term we use. That is, he asks those filing the charge, or the report, can be asked for additional information. But he might ask others for additional information, whether it be institutions or enterprises or whatever, depending on the case. For example, if it is a financial matter, he can ask the banks for additional preliminary information. Once he receives this information, he will decide what he is going to do. The third possibility provided for by the law is that he asks the court to conduct an investigation or to take investigative steps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you define which court you have in mind, because this is a specific form of continental law.

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: He asks the competent court to do this and, if we are dealing with a military court, then he will ask the military court to do so, to provide him with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What I had in mind was whether he asked the investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, he asked the investigating judge. For example, the report states that the municipal court of Brcko, the investigating judge, makes a request that a case be investigated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What about the investigating judge and the presiding judge in a court of law later on?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: According to the Law on Criminal Procedure, he plays a different role and he cannot take part in the hearing itself later on, the court hearing. His role is therefore to complete the evidence on the basis of which the perpetrator will be heard, and the witnesses and expert witnesses be heard in a court of law, in order to ascertain whether there is sufficient element to raise an indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, who decides on whether an investigation will be set into motion which represents the first step in a formal criminal procedure? Who decides this, and does Blaskic, as the commander of the Operative Zone, was he able to say that a procedure of this kind be set into motion or not?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: No. This is the exclusive right of the investigating judge, and the investigating judge passes a decision on an investigative process being set into motion. The investigating judge may not agree with the request and demand made by the Public Prosecutor. If this happens, then it goes before a council made up of three judges, a panel of three judges, which then decides whether to accept the request for a hearing or not. According to the Law on Criminal Procedure, a decision on going ahead with a hearing is brought after the perpetrator is interviewed, and only once the perpetrator is heard is the case formally opened. Or the judge can state that he does not agree, and then this comes up before a panel of judges, and the panel of judges decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The next point that I think would be relevant and merits explanation, who decides which investigative steps will be done in the case of an investigative procedure, and who can propose to a judge that certain steps be taken?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: The decision is made by the investigating judge. That is the right of the investigating judge on the basis of the Law on Criminal Procedure. The proposal is made, first of all, by the Public Prosecutor, because he has lodged the demand, the request, put in a request. Once he has put in a request, he proposes at the same time that so and so, such and such an individual be heard, that expert analysis be made, whether it be in the criminal field or the financial field, depending on the case, forensic or otherwise, depending on the case in hand. But the defence, that is to say the accused with his defence counsel, can put forward something themselves, and so can the investigating judge. They can assess that in that particular case something more must be done, for example, that the crime should be reconstructed, regardless of the fact that this was not proposed either by the Prosecutor or the defence counsel. It is the investigating judge that has the final say in this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Therefore, the investigating judge may conclude that the case has been sufficiently analysed and the facts sufficiently established to bring it to court. What happens next? What is the next step in this procedure?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: The investigating judge, once he has completed his analysis, sends the case back to the Public Prosecutor, and the Public Prosecutor, once again, has three possibilities: One is to give up any further procedure, any further prosecution, because he has assessed that the material amassed and the evidence amassed is not sufficient for conviction. Then the case is dropped. The second possibility is that the Public Prosecutor asks additional information, once again, of the investigating judge. These are rare cases, but if, in the meantime, some new knowledge comes to light, then he can ask for this additional material to be supplied. I think this is Article 158 of the Law on Criminal Procedure. I'm not quite sure which allows for this possibility. The third possibility, which is the most frequent, that is to raise an indictment against the perpetrator, to issue an indictment which is sent to the court of law.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Once again, although we see this from your context, but, as I am Defence counsel for General Blaskic and would like an answer, can Blaskic, as the head of the Operative Zone, wield any influence and can he influence the Public Prosecutor in him making his decision as to whether to issue an indictment or not?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: No, he cannot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, I would like you to get back to the essential point of our discussion here. Do you hear me, Mr. Hayman? I would like us to get back to the focus of our discussion. We want to know what was the role, the function of the military police at the time of that conflict in relation to what the accused can do. Otherwise, we are hearing a kind of course on criminal procedure, which takes me back to concepts of which we are familiar in civil law. It's very interesting, of course, but the focus of the discussion is the military police and the orders that the accused might give in wartime, in conflict time. We would like to know whether there was a failure to act properly, a failure to go to see the Prosecutor General, but all the rest really is a presentation of the civil procedures that was used for the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna. That last question seems to better focus onto what our discussion really is about. Otherwise we are going to waste time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we felt it necessary to give you the framework of criminal procedure and to show that Blaskic had no role in this, and we wanted to show that his role did not exist at any stage of the criminal procedure, and we shall, of course, be going back to the military police and show this in greater detail, but we felt that we should inform the Court of the specific features of this procedure, where it is other people altogether from the legislative system who decide whether a case is to be brought to trial or not, and this is in connection with General Blaskic. We have now arrived at the point in which we mentioned the indictment and the case and criminal proceedings, so we will end there as far as criminal procedure is concerned. I'd now like to ask that documents be handed around which concern the military police. We have a set of documents, first the Croatian text and then the English translation. They haven't been joined together, that is to say, the Croatian text is separate and the English text is separate, but they should be conjoined as one piece of evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is D522A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have the Rules and Regulations on the Establishment of the Military Police of the Croatian Armed Forces of Herceg-Bosna dating back to 1994, the regulations for the formation and work of the military police of the armed forces, and we have translated only the articles which we consider to be relevant to this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, just to note for the record, that puts us at somewhat of a disadvantage. While the Defence thinks that these particular articles that start at, I think, Article 54 may be relevant to the case, there may be other relevant articles that the Prosecutor feels are important to bring to the attention of this witness, and without a full and complete translation of that document, we are handicapped in conducting an effective cross-examination on this particular document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: How many articles are there, Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In this document, we have translated articles from Article 53 on up until Article 73 inclusive. It is a document which the Prosecution has received but probably not translated yet. As you noticed a moment ago and on several occasions, the Defence only received parts of documents, a milinfosum or some other document which the Prosecutor felt to be important, and then we only used those parts of the document that we received. Sometimes they were photocopied in such a way that only one line of the document was shown, whereas the other part was left out of the photocopied page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, while this is not a great difficulty, this isn't the first time that one of the parties, you included, considered out of an entire document one part is relevant for the cause that you are defending, I believe; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Usually, Mr. President, in that circumstance, the other side has the ability to read the document in toto. In this situation, Mr. President, where there is a portion of a document, this is only Article 53 through Article 73, I know that there are 52 articles that precede 53. I don't know how many articles go beyond 72. I don't have the ability to read those particular provisions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: My second question is simply to know whether the entire decree, from Articles 1 to 52, were all of those given to you in Serbo-Croatian, as Mr. Nobilo seems to say? Was it given to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We received this last week, Mr. President. The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That's what I thought. All right. First of all, this is not the first time that one of the parties receives an entire document, but the other party considers that, for its case, only some of the elements are relevant. It is self-evident, of course, that you can take the entire document, and I could, therefore, ask the -- or, rather, you can ask the translation service, I'll tell the Registrar, that the other relevant articles should be urgently translated so that you could know the content, and then if you need it for your cross-examination, you can have it. I'll ask that the translation service be asked to translate this material immediately. Of course, that would delay the cross-examination. Mr. Nobilo, proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I just want to note, Mr. President, our objection in the sense that the Prosecutor, not only has he given us partial translations of documents he has used in his case, he gives us partial documents. No rule of completeness has been applied by this Court to documents provided by the Prosecutor and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. I told the Prosecutor that this was not the first time, not the first time, that this has happened. That's the first of my answers, I, perhaps, should explain myself, but then I added that the party that does not know the entire document is the one that has to ensure that the document is completely translated, and I can say to the Prosecutor that that is his responsibility to have the document translated. That's all I'm saying. What's your objection, Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The Court is suggesting that the cross-examination should be delayed until some larger part of the document is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I don't know. Perhaps that won't be necessary. I'm simply saying that perhaps the cross-examination should be delayed. It is the Judges who asked you this, Mr. Hayman, I, myself, or Judge Shahabuddeen could wonder why, from Articles 1 to 52, we don't know what the context is. That is the question that the Judges could ask, and that would delay the cross-examination. I think it natural that one of the parties wants to know what is the general context of the document. You, Mr. Hayman, I'm not criticising you, I'm not criticising you, but I consider it natural for you to consider that what is relevant would be Articles 53 to 73. I'm not criticising you either insofar as you have disclosed the entire document. I made sure of that. Perhaps I might reproach the Prosecutor for not having had the entire document translated earlier, but having said this, I consider it natural that the Tribunal and the Prosecution should have the entire translation of the entire document, and I'll ask this to be translated urgently. I think that the translation service will not take a great deal of time to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If that is the rule, Mr. President, we want the entire documents of all the snippets and pieces and one lines and one paragraphs that have been given --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, Mr. Hayman, Mr. Hayman, please, please, you always try to establish rules, codes, and procedures. You are not in a specific legal system. You are in front of Judges who are trying to get to the truth of the case. Let us operate, please. Immediately, you don't have to construct a rule and a regulation. I'm not at that point. If you had asked that at one point, we would have considered that issue at another point, but for the time being, I'm simply settling this issue. You have supplied -- you are irreproachable, irreproachable, when you supplied the entire text. The Prosecutor could have -- let me finish please. I'm the one presiding here. The Prosecutor could have had the document translated earlier. He said that he was missing one day. He could have had the entire document translated earlier, but in light of the questions that you're asking, the Prosecutor is now saying to us that, in fact, he is missing Articles 1 to 52, so we're trying to resolve the problem. I've consulted Judge Shahabuddeen, and I'm trying to resolve the issue. I'm not trying to resolve all the questions since the 23rd of January, 1997. I've been trying to gain some time here. And if I were the one to ask, what would you say if I were asking that 1 to 52 be translated, and in French in addition to all that? Do I complain when I don't have the documents in French? I don't say anything. That is the end of that. I don't like people intervening once the Trial Chamber has taken a decision. I'll ask the Registry that the translation service act immediately so that, as quickly as possible, this text can be translated. That's natural. It's natural to have the context.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry I've angered you, Mr. President, if I have, but it is my duty to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The incident is closed. Yes, it is your duty, but I also have a duty, that is, to move things forward. Immediately, a rule must be constructed, that's what one asks for. I'm trying to resolve questions here. We always run into new problems in this Tribunal. Let's try to resolve them as we go along. I've never refused you a translation. Let me point that out to you. The incident is closed and the decision has been taken. The translation service will start to work on this as quickly as possible, and if the Prosecutor needs explanations of the witness by keeping the witness here, we can have him stay. We're wasting a lot of time, and we waste a lot of time on a lot of points, and I don't think that it is the Presiding Judge who is causing us to waste most of the time here. Mr. Nobilo, please ask your question. In fact, we're going to take a break now. That will calm all of us down, starting with me. A 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can now resume the hearing. Have the accused brought in, please. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: As regards the organisation of our work, we will sit until a quarter to one, and then resume at 3.00 and work until 6.00. Thank you. Will the translation be ready tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The translation will be available to the Prosecution tomorrow in the beginning of the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You see. That does not change the fact that we agree that the exhibit can be admitted. Mr. Nobilo, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have another document that is part of the regulations for the formation and work of the military police, the military police of the armed forces of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, so it is similar with D522; however, it is not in continuity with the articles that are in D522. We have separated it, and in this way, we are going to shorten the time needed for translation because we have three or four articles more there. Could be please have this document distributed to the Court and the parties? So this is a document that we'd also like to have tendered and is part of the regulations for the formation and work of the military police from 1994.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is D523A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, this document, 522 and also D523, is called "Regulations for the Formation and Work of the Military Police of the Armed Forces of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna from 1994." Please tell the Court, what is the relationship in terms of hierarchy between this legal act called the regulations and the legal act which is called the law? So what is the relationship in terms of hierarchy between the Law on Criminal Procedure on the one hand and the regulations on the formation and work of the military police on the other hand?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: The Law on Criminal Procedure has absolute supremacy over the regulations. The regulations are a lower legal act. If this lower legal act is not in compliance with the law, then the law is overriding.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Am I right if I say that the lower act would have to correspond to the institutes of the higher act?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Now, I would like to read a few sections of the regulations to you, and then I would like to put a question to you. I would like to find a connection with the law. I'm referring to Article 12 of D523: "While accomplishing the tasks from the sphere of actions, authorised official persons from the military police have and apply the same authorities that, by the regulations that determine the criminal procedure, have the authorised bodies of the Ministry of Internal Affairs of Croatian Republic of HB and authorised official persons from the police." So I would like to ask you the following: As it says here in Article 12, regulations concerning the military police, what did the legislator have in mind when using this, that is to say, regulations that determine the criminal procedure?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: This Article 12 refers to regulations from the Law on Criminal Procedure, that is to say, the Law on Criminal Procedure regulated in detail how authorised persons would act within criminal procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I wish to draw your attention to document D522, Article 53, and I'm reading it out: "The military police service for fighting crime consists of a number of jobs and tasks which, by the law which determines the criminal procedure, are being done by the offices of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, and they are related to criminal actions which go under the jurisdiction of military courts, and they are: 1) Criminal acts that are committed by military persons; 2) Criminal acts that were committed by officers and employees in military forces while doing their service or in connection with their service and for other criminal acts that they commit as coexecutors together with military persons; 3) Criminal acts that were committed by civilians but go under the jurisdiction of the military court." Again, my question is, is this norm directly related to the provisions of the Law on Criminal Procedure that you spoke of, and is it in conformity with the Law on Criminal Procedure?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes. This Article 53 is a norm which is in line with the Law on Criminal Procedure, and it directly pertains to the powers that are envisaged by the Law on Criminal Procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Now let us repeat this: The Law on Criminal Procedure, does it allow the commander of the Operative Zone to command the military police in terms of what are going to be the investigative or pre-investigative actions that they will take?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: No, that is not within his authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The next article, Article 55, in this same document, D522, I would like to draw your attention to that: "Actions from Article 54 of this book of regulations are being done ex officio by the authorised official person from the unit of the military police that has the jurisdiction under the territorial division and on the request of the authorised state attorney or the court." This provision of the regulations, that is to say, Article 55, does it also reflect what you spoke of, as you were commenting on the Law on Criminal Procedure when you said who can exercise influence over the military police in terms of the things that they can do?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes. This provision contained in Article 55 is one that also addresses itself to the Law on Criminal Procedure, and, with your permission, perhaps it should be stated here, that the decree on the establishment of district military courts, I don't know exactly, but I think that it is Article 25, it specifically stipulates that the internal affairs authority is equated with the security authorities in the armed forces. The district military court is equal to a regular first instance court, and the district military prosecutor with the senior prosecutor, that is to say, the republican prosecutor as far as certain powers are concerned, that is to say, those stemming from the Law on Criminal Procedure. So this decree speaks for itself, that these are powers enjoyed by the authorities from the Ministry of Internal Affairs and the security services in the case of war and, in this case, this is the military police, that is to say, the section that dealt with crime investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly? Are you trying to say that when the military police acts as a crime investigation police does, then they have to act in accordance with the Law on Criminal Procedure?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. Several decrees that were passed, including the decree on military courts, as well as the decree on the application of the Law on Criminal Procedure during war, in cases of imminent danger of war, state this explicitly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Articles 69, 70, 71, I don't really have to read all of them out, but could you take a look at them, and could you say whether they fully elaborate on the Law on Criminal Procedure, and are they fully in accordance with the role of the police according to the Law on Criminal Procedure? So would you please read Article 69, 70, and 71?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, this is a consistent transcription, so to speak, of the Law on Criminal Procedure, that is to say, regulating the relationship between the civilian police and the public prosecutor, and that is what I stated in my introductory remarks, that is to say, the police vis-a-vis the public prosecutor in terms of filing criminal reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I should like to draw your attention to something else, I'm going to read it to you, and I believe that this is the only one that refers to the military commander, and that is Article 73 of the regulations, that is, D522, and I'm reading it out now: "The commanders of the units and all the members of the Croatian Defence Council are obliged to, within their rights and obligations, give necessary help to authorised official persons from the military police and enable them to collect information and accomplish other acts that are mentioned in the Law on Criminal Procedure." So could you please tell me your opinion? What duty is prescribed for a military commander, in this particular case, Blaskic? How would you interpret this provision?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: It says there that all citizens and institutions, enterprises, et cetera, are duty-bound to assist the police, authorised official persons, in terms of bringing to justice and to a court of law the perpetrators of criminal offences. Here it has been translated into military conditions, which would mean that the commander of a unit, as well as others within military units, are duty-bound to help the military police and its crime investigation section in terms of operative work involved in collecting evidence concerning a particular crime. We can illustrate this by the following: To give them insight into documents; to allow them to enter or tour certain facilities; also giving them access to certain persons, letting them question certain persons from military units; then providing them with technical assistance, so whatever the police would do, in terms of crime investigation and in terms of collecting evidence. That would be the duty of a military commander as well as others in a military structure. Because the military police, that is to say, its section that relates to security, has wide powers and they are even entitled to question the commander himself and to look into his responsibility too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I think that there is a bit, or perhaps even more than a bit, perhaps this is a substantial mistake in the interpretation. So could you repeat once again what is the duty of the military commander? Does he have certain powers over the military police or does he have other duties? Please, would you repeat this once again slowly.

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: It is the duty of the military commander, first and foremost, to help the crime investigation police and to put at their disposal whatever they require. That is to say to provide them with certain documents, to allow them access in terms of certain facilities, to question certain witnesses that are under the command of that commander, that is to say within his hierarchy, and also to give them technical assistance, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Does every citizen have that kind of obligation, every owner of an enterprise, everybody according to the Law on Criminal Procedure?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the very outset I said that this provision does exist in the Law on Criminal Procedure; however, naturally, it does not mention the army. It says that every citizen, authorised person, institution of the state, enterprises, are duty-bound to help find the perpetrators of criminal acts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Now let us go back to document D521. Let us look at Article 27, the only one where the commander is mentioned. These are special provisions related to district military courts. Again, it is a decree with the force of a law of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna on district military courts during the situation of war or imminent danger of war. I am going to read this entire article to you, and I would like to ask you to give me your views on this. This is the only one where explicit mention is made of the commander. So I am reading Article 27: "The commander of a military unit or military establishment shall take every possible measure to prevent the perpetrator of a criminal offence who is prosecuted ex officio from hiding or escaping, to preserve the traces of the criminal offence and objects which may serve as evidence, and shall gather all information which may be of use for the conducting of criminal proceedings. The commander of the unit or establishment shall immediately inform the district military prosecutor or his immediate superior commanding officer of the data referred to in paragraph 1 of this article. The report of the commander referred to in paragraph 2 of this article may be used in the manner envisaged in the provisions of Articles 84 through 86 of the Law on Criminal Procedure. A military commander holding the post of company commander, an equivalent or higher post or an authorised official of the Department of the Interior and the security department, or the military police, may arrest a member of the military in cases envisaging detention under the Law on Criminal Procedure. The commander and the authorised official referred to in paragraph 1 of this article shall immediately, and at the latest within 12 hours, surrender the member of the military whom they have arrested, together with a report on the reasons for his detention with evidence to the investigative judge of the competent district military court or to the nearest military unit and/or military establishment which shall immediately bring him before the competent investigative judge of the district military court. If the military commander or the authorised official are unable to do this, they shall forthwith, and within eight hours at the latest, inform the investigative judge of the competent district military court or the nearest military unit or the military establishment of which the arrested person is a member to immediately take charge of him and without delay escort him to the nearest competent investigative judge of a district military court." My first question would be the following: Does this relate to a known person when the perpetrator is known or is the commander supposed to investigate on his own whether somebody committed a crime or not? What do you think?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: Well, judging by the context of Article 27, its norm, it proceeds from the assumption that the perpetrator of the mentioned crime is known, and that this person should be detained, all the traces kept, and this person should be surrendered to the military police or, rather, the investigative judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Give me an example, please, an imaginary example. In which cases could there be this kind of a situation that the military commander, for example Colonel Blaskic, is duty-bound to detain a person and to make sure that all the evidence is there? What case, for example?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: I shall quote an example. For example, let us say that a murder was committed in his unit and that everyone knows who did it, because it happened there. The perpetrator is detained, all the traces are kept, also the crime scene remains intact. They wait for the police to come, the investigative judge and the Public Prosecutor, and then the entire case is handed over to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we please have another document distributed now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is D524, 524A for the French version and B for the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: May we identify the document. We discussed it, that is to say you discussed it. So could you just identify it and tell us what it represents, this new document.

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: This is the regulation, the decree by which the application of the Criminal Code of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Criminal Code of the SFRY, Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, in the time of the immediate threat of war or in time of war on the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Another question now, and this would be the last question in that block of questions. We have seen the formation of the military courts and Prosecutor's offices in Bosnia-Herzegovina and what their relationship was with the commander to the Operative Zone. I would now like to ask you the following: In the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was there any other solution, and if there was, could you describe it to us briefly, what the relationship there was like between the commander of the corps and the legal organs active for his territory.

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: The presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina enacted, as I've already said, a provision on the founding of military law courts for the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and they are the seven courts that I enumerated earlier on. However, in addition to that decree, the presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina enacted a second decree on special or separate military courts. The characteristics of this decree and the differences from the first decree is the following: According to the first decree that was enacted, the military courts were, hierarchially speaking, organisationally speaking, one of the organisation of the Defence ministry, that is to say under their supervision, and the presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina appointed judges. According to the second decree, we have a purely military component. In this second decree the commanders of the military units, as far as I remember, and I think that I even have the documents somewhere with me, that the commander of the brigade or lower down echelon, the military echelon, could form a military court. In that case he would be responsible to it, that is to say he would be the individual appointing the judges. That is the so-called decree on special or separate military courts. I think that it was published in the Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Take a look at your notes. Feel free to do so, if you need a date or a figure.

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: In Official Gazette No. 12/92 of the 13th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: That refers to the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, does it not?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, it refers exclusively to the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: May we now move onto the last area, the system by which criminal sanctions are put into effect. What law was prevalent in Bosnia-Herzegovina up until the war and what were the solutions in the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna? What solutions were found in view of the types of detention centres or gaols and how criminal sanctions were executed?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: Bosnia-Herzegovina had its own laws on the execution of criminal sanctions. It had these before the war, and it was the prevailing law on the basis of which all sentences were executed, had institutions for the execution of prison sentences, and other institutions, forensic institutions, institutions for minors and so on. The presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina also, when the war broke out, enacted a decree on the application of this law in a state of war. The characteristics of that particular decree which came into force in a situation of war was that within the frameworks of the existing gaols or detention centres, departments were set up for a military prisons. Within the frameworks of the penitentiaries or detention centres, there were departments or special units for military convicts. Identical solutions existed in the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, once again on the basis of a decree. In both systems, and in the district military courts, a detention was provided for. That is to say that is the phase while the investigation is being conducted and before sentence is actually being passed and judgment passed. The perpetrator then goes to the district prisons and the penitentiaries, or houses of correction, where there were special units for military personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: If I have understood you correctly, there are civilian detention centres for individuals whose trials are ongoing, and then there are military detention centres for military individuals who are undergoing a trial, and a prison for criminal sanctions with both civilian units and military units?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could you now tell the Court something about the individual types of detention centres or prisons. Under which ministry did they fall? Who was the authority over these prisons?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: By decree this question was regulated for the military prisons, military detention. It was the district military court that was in charge of these centres and supervision was the defence department, which was later to become the Ministry of Defence. When it came to prison sentences, supervision was done by the defence department and, as I say, later on it became the Ministry of Defence. It was quite separate, in the sense of supervision from the civilian section. Civilian section came under the Ministry of Justice, whereas the Ministry of Defence was in charge of the military units.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Therefore, both categories of detainees or prisoners were under the control and supervision and administration of two ministries, the Ministry of Defence and the Ministry of Justice, the Ministry of Justice for civilians and the Ministry of Defence for the soldiers. When you say Ministry of Defence, do you consider that this was the civilian section of the Ministry of Defence or the military units and military commanders of the Operative Zones? Did the military commanders of the Operative Zones have any supervision over military detention centres?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: We are talking about the civilian part of the Ministry of Defence, so the Ministry of Defence was the executive power and within the frameworks of its competencies and authorisations it had other segments. One of those segments was the main staff and, for example, the chief of the military police and so on. So this belonged to the civilian section of that ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I would now like to ask, although it does emanate from your question, a direct question. Did Blaskic, according to any basis, was he authorised to control or command what was happening in a military detention centre or military prison?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: No, that was not his competence or authority. I am just looking through the decree you have tendered into evidence, which states precisely that supervision is -- that the Department of Defence, which was later the Ministry of Defence, was in charge of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You are talking about the decree on military courts of law?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I would now like to have a new document handed out. This document has been translated only into French. That's how we received it from the interpretation and translation services. It is very short and I would like to read it out so that everybody can hear.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is D525. A for the French version.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I am going to read it out, because there isn't an English translation. The preamble: "On the basis of Article 7, paragraph 2 of the decision on the establishment of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna dated the 18th of November, 1991, the presidency of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna at its session of the 3rd of July, 1992 adopts the following decree." It is the decree relative to the treatment of individuals taken prisoner in armed conflicts in the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, Article 1. "The members of the JNA and the reserve formations of the JNA and all other persons taken prisoner in the armed conflicts against the community of Herceg-Bosna (prisoners in the HZHB) the regulations of the Geneva Conventions shall be applied relevant to prisoners of war of the 12th of August, 1949." And in brackets it states: "The Official Gazette of the SFRY," and the number is 24/1950. Article 2: "The chief of the justice department and administration department in co-operation with the chief of the defence department and the chief of the interior affairs department shall determine the location and locations in which in keeping with the Geneva Conventions, as mentioned in Article 1 of this provision, the prisoners shall be detained." Article 3: "The defence department shall administer these locales related to Article 2 of this decree." Article 4: "This decree comes into force on the day of its adoption." The signatures, the President of the HVO and HZHB, Mate Boban, and on other the side it states the Republic of Bosnia-Hercegovina, the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, the presidency and the number, Mostar the 3rd of July, '92. I should now like to ask you to comment on this document and how the question of prisoners of war was determined, who determined where they would be located, who was in charge of the localities where the prisoners of war were located, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: Bearing in mind the provisions of the Geneva Conventions on the treatment of prisoners of war dated the 12th of August, 1949, this provision was enacted, this decree was enacted as soon as the armed conflict broke out, that is to say, at the beginning of July, with the aim of respecting the provisions of the Geneva Conventions, and in that sense, three departments were placed in charge of these affairs in the organisation as it existed in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, that was the justice department, the defence department, and the internal affairs department, that is to say, the police, that locations be set for the temporary detention of prisoners of war in conformity with the provisions of the conventions. The important fact to note here and in regard to this decree, in addition to the fact that the decree had to be applied and the convention had to be applied, is that the administration, supervision, and control was in the hands of the defence department in the organisation of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and that was under their jurisdiction, whereas the two other departments, only in a certain way, were a support and helped localities to be found and pinpointed for situations of this kind to be used for purposes of detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: According to your knowledge, did the military commanders, under the main staff, including Blaskic as the commander of the Operative Zone, were they, in any way, authorised to meddle and to interfere into the affairs of organisation and location of the prisoners of war, and did they have any authorisations and competencies over the prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: No. That was not under their competence or this was not the competence of the commanders, and the decree took it out of their hands, so to speak, and that is how things stood, so that Mr. Blaskic had no authorisations in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: According to your recollections and knowledge, you were not the justice minister in 1993, you were appointed minister in 1994, sometime in March, but according to your recollections and knowledge, did the military court in Travnik and the military prosecutor's office in Travnik function normally in the course of 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: I said in my introduction today, I said a number of sentences on the difficulties that the courts found themselves faced with in functioning throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina, and regardless of the fact that I was not in Mostar, I was at the time in the northern parts of Bosnia, in Bosanska Posavina at the time, I was in constant contact and communication because I was detached. And my duties were to go to Posavina to set up the legal system there, and I know that it was a very difficult situation. There were no cadres, not enough cadres, not enough conditions for the functioning of law courts.
