utterances.text: What type of ammunition were the HVO using in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about the HVO in Bosnia. I am a professor in Zagreb and had contacts with the Croatian army, and everything that I said is relevant for the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you cannot tell the Judges anything about the type of ammunition that was fired on the 18th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Only what I read in those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Professor, did you, in the process of your calculations, travel to the site in Zenica to assess the geography and see the impact sites?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I did not need to. Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the best witnesses in respect of an incident such as this are individuals who were present at the time of this shelling and who gave eyewitness accounts to the Court?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I am speaking about mathematics here, about calculations. I don't know what I could say about witnesses who were on site. I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You didn't answer my question. Do you not believe that experts who are on site in Zenica, on the day of this incident, military personnel from all over the world, can give a better insight to the Judges of what actually happened?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: What I read in this material, these texts, are things that I don't agree with. That's the only thing I can say. I can't give you an opinion about something I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Which witnesses did you have the occasion to read make when you made your study of the Zenica shelling?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I read the text of the Major, Witness V and Witness W.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Professor, have you ever been involved in the process of crater analysis in your career?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, very frequently. I looked at craters very often on the firing ranges.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that crater analysis can provide a good indication of the type of projectile, the calibre of the projectile, and the bearing, the direction from which the projectile was fired?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have read many things about that and I prepared myself to reach a similar conclusion. The determination of the calibre and direction and the angle of fall starting from a crater is something I have never seen discussed in scientific or technical literature. Therefore, this is not a problem which is resolved in advance, but rather problems that technicians and people have to resolve on site with the knowledge that they have. Therefore, in practice, through tests on the firing ranges, we record what the effects are, that is, what is the crater produced by a given projectile. We know the projectile that we are using to fire, and through tests we can note what crater it produces in the firing range, and we consider that to be the performance of that projectile of that object. As regards the contrary, that's a very great problem for which I do not have a solution, but it must be said that when we look at the fragments and the pieces of projectile, we can recognise the projectile that fell ordinarily through large pieces, that is, that very often, the rocket remains in one piece and that the base, the base of the projectile, produces large pieces, and one can recognise those pieces as parts of projectiles. That's possible and that's done, but you have to be careful here as well because the same rocket can use several shells. For instance, the rocket RGM, there's a similar Yugoslav version, that rocket uses 122-millimetres, that's the howitzer that we're speaking about. It also uses 130 guns and 152 howitzer guns, therefore, all three, that's one thing, and one has to be careful.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Professor, let me just interrupt. Mr. President, at the beginning of this paragraph, I think the word "inverse" was translated as "contrary." In the French, I'm pretty sure it was inverse. The professor was talking about whether you could reason in both directions, that is, from a known shell to a characteristic, but then he commented on the inverse, from the characteristic back to the shell. In the English translation, it was translated as "the contrary." I think it's "the inverse."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Converse.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Inverse or converse.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Converse.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: It was translated as "the contrary."

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I have to say, Mr. President, I didn't spot that. All I've spotted is that Mr. Hayman and I have been confused on the transcript, and it's now referring to Mr. Cayley as Mr. Hayman, but that's a small point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, the inverse or converse?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'll ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let's do it again. Do you want to make a correction? Converse, inverse?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: May I answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, specify, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: To be very precise, for a given projectile, the tests determine the crater, and we know that the projectile produces this or that crater, and that crater could have been produced by another projectile, but we will never go from a crater to say what crater it was that produced it, but we know that a projectile produced the crater.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Let's move along, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Professor, you studied the testimony of Major Baggesen, and would you agree with me that he assessed the direction of fire as 270 degrees?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't answer that, and I'll explain why. Whenever I look at a crater, I look at the earth, I don't look at the crater on an asphalt surface. We don't do that in technical studies. I have never seen craters of this type, and I can't answer that question. And the photos that I saw were unusable. They were not oriented in such a way that one could say whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Photographs can only be used for illustrative purposes, can't they, Professor? You cannot calculate range and bearing from a photograph, can you? It's very difficult.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand what you said. I said that, according to the copies of the photographs that I looked at, I can't say anything about the direction on asphalt, and especially because, in practice, I have never seen a crater produced on asphalt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: If you prefer to speak in your own language, of course, Professor, you can, because you seem to say that you don't understand what Mr. Cayley is saying, and I'm very sensitive to the fact that you're speaking in French. Perhaps it would be better for you to speak in your own language, and then the interpreters will interpret, but you can do as you like. I'm only making a comment to try to facilitate things, if you say you didn't understand what you were asked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's to understand the question. It's not a question of the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, no, I understand, but perhaps if you were to keep your answers --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were many technical terms. The interpretation sometimes takes a little longer to come out. That's all. I'm only trying to understand the question well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Do as you like. Do as you like. Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I just wish to say the following: We talked to the witness, and he said that he wanted to answer in French, and the Defence thought that this was necessary, and this is obviously so. With all due respect to the interpreters, who do a splendid job as far as legal terms are concerned, but I must say that the translation into Croatian is not perfectly clear, so it's important for you, as the Presiding Judge, to get it all right in French, and if the Defence doesn't get it all right in Croatian, it's of lesser importance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Professor, it is far easier to make an assessment from a crater on range and bearing if you are actually present, compared to purely using photographic material; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. You said two things, that you want to make an evaluation on the basis of a crater, an evaluation of the range and the direction. The first question is not possible to answer. One cannot evaluate the range on the basis of the crater. I don't believe one can. That's my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You misunderstood my question, Professor --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: And the second question that you asked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting. You didn't understand the question. We want to move things forward. You see, there is a comprehension problem here. Prosecution counsel is asking you whether it's easier to make an evaluation from a photograph or from on-site observations. That's the question.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: As I said to you, I had to understand the translation properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, exactly, but he also added the range and the direction, and then the professor said that the range cannot be ascertained on the basis of the crater at all, and probably he's going to continue now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, first let's try to understand the questions so that we can understand the answers better. Please do not give an additional interpretation of what your witness is saying. He's big enough to know what he has to say. All right. Ask your question again, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We'll break it down and put it in a more straightforward fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In terms of crater analysis, Professor, is it easier to make observations of a crater on the site or from photographic material?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: On-site.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you studied the testimony of Major Baggesen, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You would agree with me that he came to the conclusion that the angle of fire was 270 degrees. That was his testimony, wasn't it, Professor?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I read that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: He also assessed the size of the artillery shell as being a 122-millimetre shell, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let me remind you. Again, these transcript references may not be correct because I, apparently having spoken to my learned friend, Mr. Hayman, have a slightly different edition than he. On page 1.939: "We discussed and we concluded that it had to be medium artillery, that is, 122-millimetre artillery." Do you recall reading that, Professor?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I had the material starting with page 2.112.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you didn't consider the examination-in-chief of Major Baggesen in giving your presentation today to the Court?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I prepared starting from page 2.112.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Would it surprise you to know, Professor, that you don't have all of Major Baggesen's testimony?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you not think you would have been able to give better observations to the Court if you had had the complete transcript of Major Baggesen's testimony about the Zenica shelling?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I've given my opinion based on what I read. I didn't need anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you're stating to the Judges that you believe that you can give your expert opinion on the incomplete testimony of an expert eyewitness to the shelling of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how to answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness has answered this, and now repeating these questions makes no sense. If the Prosecutor wishes to do so, he can quote Major Baggesen, and then he's going to present his opinion, but why repeat it time and again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, I don't think that's right. I think that the Prosecutor is following a plan. Continue, Mr. Cayley. I think it is almost 6.00, but continue for a few more moments, and then the case will continue tomorrow. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you believe that you would have been able to give a better opinion to the Judges had Mr. Nobilo provided you with the complete testimony of Major Baggesen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, he answered that question, Mr. Cayley. Now there I agree with Mr. Nobilo. He answered. He said that the elements that he had were enough for him in order to give an answer. Move to another question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you read the part of Major Baggesen's testimony where he assessed the range to be 15 kilometres; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you think it would have been helpful to you in your testimony here today had you been provided with that piece of evidence that Major Baggesen provided to the Court?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't need anything more than what I already had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Cayley, you received that answer already. The witness is satisfied with the materials that he had and that he read. You can cross-examine him on those things that he read.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is actually a different point. This is a different piece of information which the witness did not have, and I think it's a fairly serious matter, if a witness is coming in here to comment upon evidence and he's commenting on an incomplete file of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. All right. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this point, we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. I'll let you make your evaluation. All right. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The point that I'm making, Mr. President, is that it appears the witness had not been provided with all of the evidence of Major Baggesen. Now, he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, we know that now. Go ahead. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm simply stating to the Court, and perhaps it's a matter for final argument, that I think that that is a fairly serious matter, since he is only commenting on written evidence that he has been provided with.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Well, since we're discussing that matter, Mr. President, Major Baggesen did not undertake a ballistics study. Witness W did. Major Baggesen did not undertake a ballistics study. He did not. He made no mathematical calculations.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: It's apples and oranges, and counsel can argue in closing argument, but if we're going to argue the issue, then let's have both sides argue it because we have something to say about that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, no. First of all, we're not trying to accuse anybody of anything here. We will resume tomorrow at 2.00. I would like to point out to Mr. Cayley that it's three times now that we -- there are two things. First of all, the witness did not have all of the testimony, and you can draw all the conclusions you like from that, but the second thing is we know that the witness found enough material in what was given to him in order to do his calculations. From that point on, you can continue. Perhaps you can ask one or two questions on this subject before we end for this evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm probably going to be moving to another witness's testimony, so now would be a convenient time to pause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. I think so too. We can resume tomorrow at 2.00 for the continuation of the cross-examination. First, we'll begin with the cross-examination of this witness, Mr. Jankovic, before we move to the cross-examination of the previous witness. All right. The Court stands adjourned. We will resume tomorrow at 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
